newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FORECAST - Dutch Q2 GDP seen bringing strong rise.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Dutch Q2 GDP seen bringing strong rise.

text.p: Dutch gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to rise 2.6 percent in the second quarter, and some analysts said on Tuesday they did not rule out an even stronger 3.0-percent jump, fuelled by strong consumption.

In a Reuters poll on Tuesday of four major banks, economists' estimates for second-quarter GDP ranged between 2.5 and 2.8 percent year-on-year, after a 1.8-percent rise in the first three months of 1996. GDP data are due on Thursday.
These predictions were well above those made in March, when disappointing German growth triggered downgrades of Dutch GDP growth to 1.0 to 1.5 percent for the full year.
The Dutch economy is also in much better shape than neighbouring economies in Germany, Belgium and France where 1996 GDP growth was seen between 0.5 and 1.1 percent in 1996.
Dutch consumer spending, which makes up 60 percent of GDP, has dragged the economy out of its trough and was seen spurring the growth.
April consumer spending rose 2.9 percent and 4.4 percent in May. June's figure on Thursday was also expected to be strong.
"It wouldn't surprise me if second-quarter GDP comes out at a three-percent rise. The CBS has already hinted that Thursday could bring a big figure," said ABN AMRO economist Nico Klene.
Other factors behind the upturn of the Dutch economy from its virtual standstill in the last quarter of 1995 include a replenishing of low inventories and continued exports strength.
The pick-up has created a windfall for the government, which can use extra tax income to cut the national debt, a crucial item in the run-up to the single European currency.

"The government budgeted with a cautious two-percent GDP growth a year when it took office two years ago. It will be a big relief that full-year growth is again expected to be above that level in the third year," said Fred Pallada at ING Barings.
Economists now expect full-year growth of 2.5-2.6 percent.
But they expected consumer spending alone would no longer lead the growth in the second half.

"Due to modest wage deals, the purchasing power of consumers does not rise by the four percent we have seen in spending. The recent increase in consumption is partly paid by savings and borrowings, which will stop at some time," Klene said.
Real family income rose by 3.6 percent in 1995, but consumption rose only 2.1 percent in the same year, with the difference often put into tax-deductible saving schemes.
These savings were stashed away for four years, but some has been put into housing, fuelling the housing boom.
Housing shortages have driven prices up by 47 percent since 1991 while mortgages are at all-time lows, allowing many people to raise their mortgage to pay for interior decorating.
Decorating and furniture retailers reported booming business as people, leaving behind expensive property, were tempted by banks to borrow additional money for home improvement.
All this spending is included in consumption.
"So far, mortgage loans have risen by 12.5 percent this year, which is even more than last year. This has really surprised us and could explain the high consumption growth," Pallada said.
